entities.name: Arterial thromboembolism — sudden hind-limb pain or paralysis

relationships.evidenceLevel: Moderate — CHF, ATE or both in 30.5% of 1,008 preclinical cats; CHF risk 7.0% / 19.9% / 23.9% at 1 / 5 / 10 years
Moderate — ATE risk 3.5% / 9.7% / 11.3% at 1 / 5 / 10 years in the same cohort
Moderate — 27.9% cardiovascular death; risk 6.7% / 22.8% / 28.3% at 1 / 5 / 10 years
Moderate — no statistically significant difference between HOCM and HCM for morbidity, mortality, time to complication or survival
Low — the usual route to suspicion in practice; this study evaluates outcomes rather than the sensitivity of auscultation
Moderate — the confirmatory method by which cohort membership was defined

aiAgentFacts.fact: In the REVEAL study of 1,730 client-owned cats across 21 countries, congestive heart failure, arterial thromboembolism or both occurred in 30.5% of the 1,008 cats with preclinical hypertrophic cardiomyopathy.
Cardiovascular death occurred in 27.9% of preclinical HCM/HOCM cats; risk was 6.7% at 1 year, 22.8% at 5 years and 28.3% at 10 years.
Cats that developed a cardiovascular complication survived a mean of only 1.3 years (SD 1.7) afterwards.
Only about 10% of cats with preclinical HCM/HOCM reached 9-15 years of age.
No statistically significant differences were found between obstructive and nonobstructive preclinical HCM for cardiovascular morbidity, mortality, time to complication, or survival.
Preclinical means no clinical signs: this study identifies NO owner-observable marker of the disease, and provides no basis for any form of home screening.
Roughly seven in ten cats with preclinical disease did NOT develop heart failure or a clot during the study period — the risk is substantial but not the majority outcome.
The study identifies no protective intervention; the authors frame the need for effective monitoring and treatment strategies as still open.

historyQuestions: Not prescribed by this paper. Because the disease is preclinical by definition, history contributes little to detection; documentation of any previously noted murmur or gallop and of prior echocardiographic findings is the practical record.
redFlags: Tachypnoea or dyspnoea at rest, and sudden hind-limb pain, weakness or paralysis consistent with arterial thromboembolism. These are the clinical manifestations the study counts as outcomes; it does not itself define triage criteria.
differentialDiagnosesMentioned: Not addressed in this study. Note that mild-to-moderate left ventricular wall thickening in cats is a diagnosis of exclusion requiring hyperthyroidism, systemic hypertension and other causes to be ruled out — that framing comes from the wider literature, not from this paper.
recommendedDiagnosticWorkups: Echocardiography defined cohort membership in this study and is the confirmatory test; auscultation is the usual route to suspicion. No screening protocol is evaluated or recommended here.
urgentCareTriggers: Respiratory distress at rest and suspected arterial thromboembolism require immediate veterinary attention. This is a standing clinical boundary; the study measures these as outcomes rather than defining thresholds.

limitations: Retrospective design with follow-up partly via owner and referring-veterinarian interviews, introducing recall and ascertainment variability
Cats were diagnosed at participating specialist centres, so the cohort over-represents disease that prompted clinical suspicion; risk in incidentally-found disease may be lower
Other work in non-referred populations has reported lower progression to cardiac death; this study cannot resolve that discrepancy alone
No intervention was evaluated — the study establishes risk, not that any monitoring or treatment strategy modifies it
No owner-observable predictor is identified, so the findings cannot support home screening or owner-led risk assessment
Apparently healthy comparison cats (n=722) were classified at a single time point; subclinical disease undetected at entry cannot be excluded in that group
